Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. "Not organized yet" beats "not organized." The 0 to 4 tally stays folded and private. Students with ADHD gain the most from offloading; say it plainly and kindly.

Every student in the room

A system shouldn't need money or a quiet room, and family, work and faith commitments go on the calendar first, the same as practice.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can name the three skills behind getting things done (working memory, inhibition, flexibility), explain why sleep and stress change how organized anyone looks, and leave with a five-line system that moves the job out of their head: one capture point, a room set up against distraction, a plan B, and a weekly review.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 6 minThree myths, one per slide
  2. 4 minThree skills, not one
  3. 4 minA tired brain, and offload more
  4. 5 minWhere does it all live? Turn and talk, share out
  5. 10 minWhich skill needs the backup? Dev, Maya, Luis
  6. 5 minThe weekly review
  7. 6 minDesign your system: five lines
  8. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two myths, three skills, offload more, one overloaded week, the weekly review, and five lines.

Before you teach
Assume students with ADHD and learning differences are in the room.

Some have a diagnosis and a learning plan, some are waiting on an evaluation, and some have never been checked. Never ask who has ADHD or who has a plan. Talk about executive function as skills everyone uses, with some brains working harder at them.

Drop the word "lazy."

Many 9th graders have already heard "you're so capable" in that tone. If a student calls themselves lazy or bad at school, name the condition instead: short sleep, a hard week, a missing system. Keep it off any one student's record in front of the class.

Home responsibilities stay private.

Some students watch siblings, work, or travel between two homes. The system card goes home with them. Nobody explains why their afternoons are full.

If a student says "I've always been like this."

Thank them and point them to a counselor or learning specialist after class. That's where a learning plan conversation starts.

Stress and sleep can be the bigger story.

If a student describes not sleeping, feeling hopeless about school, or seeing themselves as a failure, follow up privately and bring in a counselor. Don't ask about any of this in class.

Keep the phone research honest.

The 2009 Stanford multitasking study hasn't always repeated in later work. Present it as a warning sign. The cost of switching tasks is the well-established part, and it's enough. Skip the phone lecture; students tune out fast.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Fixed blocks look different in every home.

Some students pick up a sibling, watch younger cousins until a grandparent gets home, or split the week between two homes with two calendars. Treat these as the frame the plan fits around. The Maya scenario is built for this.

A system shouldn't cost money or space.

A paper list is free and works. Not every student has a desk, a quiet room, or a phone that can live in another room. "Design the room" can mean headphones, the library before school, or the phone face down in a backpack.

ADHD and learning differences.

ADHD is largely a difference in executive function and has nothing to do with intelligence or effort. More outside structure helps. Some families are wary of evaluations or labels; present an evaluation as information that can open supports like a learning plan, and leave the decision with the student and family.

Faith commitments are fixed blocks too.

Religious services, holy days, and evening classes at a faith community belong on the calendar first, the same as practice. For students without those, the review step simply skips it.

Asking a teacher for help varies by upbringing.

In some homes questioning an adult or asking for an extension feels disrespectful. Model the exact words for "email a teacher now" so it reads as planning ahead, which most teachers welcome.

Language at home.

Some students translate forms and emails for their family, which is one more thing to track. If an evaluation comes up, families can ask the school for an interpreter. The take-home sheet is in plain language they can share.

What the research says

College students given a set of thinking tasks showed three related but separate abilities: updating (working memory), inhibition, and shifting (flexibility).

Miyake et al., Cognitive Psychology, 2000

Four things reliably weaken executive function: stress, poor sleep, loneliness, and lack of exercise.

Diamond, Annual Review of Psychology, 2013

Scanning the same young people every two years from childhood into their early 20s, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was among the last areas to mature, finishing at the end of adolescence.

Gogtay et al., PNAS, 2004

The Dunedin study followed about 1,000 New Zealanders from birth to 32. Childhood self-control predicted adult health, finances, and run-ins with the law, even after accounting for IQ and family income.

Moffitt et al., PNAS, 2011

In the same study, people whose self-control improved over time did better as adults than their childhood scores predicted.

Moffitt et al., PNAS, 2011

Heavy media multitaskers were worse at filtering out distractions and slower at switching tasks than light multitaskers. Later studies haven't all found the same thing; the cost of switching tasks is well established.

Ophir, Nass and Wagner, PNAS, 2009 (Stanford)
